blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en:
Introduction: Crop disease studies that fuse images with environmental
sensor readings, such as soil chemistry, report higher accuracy than image-only
models. In a paired image–sensor dataset, however, one reading can be attached to
many images of a session, which is one farm or greenhouse on one day. If disease
classes differ between sessions, the reading can predict the class by identifying the
session rather than by measuring the plant’s environment. Methods: We tested whether the sensor readings of two Korean datasets
identify the session, using a diagnostic that reads no image. The datasets are the Crop Disease Diagnosis (CDD) challenge dataset and a
subtropical and tropical crop pest and disease dataset from the government portal
AI Hub. The diagnostic
counts how many images share each sensor reading and compares a classifier given the sensor readings with one given
only the date and time that the dataset records. We
also re-analyzed a published CDD fusion study and trained its fusion model on the
AI Hub dataset. Results: In both datasets, nearly every image shared its sensor reading
with other images. On the AI Hub dataset, the date and time alone were comparable
to or better than the dataset’s soil-chemistry readings at predicting the disease
class in all 7 crops that we compared. For 91.9% of the CDD
study’s test images, a training image carried identical sensor readings. On the
study’s split, the date and time alone matched the study’s reported macro-F1 for
its fusion model. Trained for the study’s 300 epochs, the
fusion model raised macro-F1 slightly relative to an image-only model on a random
split of the AI Hub dataset, but whether the gain exceeds zero on
held-out dates remained unresolved. Discussion: A fusion gain measured on a split that shares sessions
between training and test data cannot be separated from session identity. Fusion
studies should therefore report the gain on a split that holds out whole farms or
sessions, and should set a sensor-only score beside those of two predictors that
read no sensor: one given only the date and time and one that always outputs the
most frequent class. Keywords: plant disease detection, multimodal fusion, environmental sensors, data leakage, shortcut learning, cross-validation, benchmark datasets

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Plant pathogens and pests reduce the yields of the major food crops worldwide [ 1 ] . To detect plant diseases, deep convolutional networks have been trained to
recognize them in leaf images [ 2 ] . Recent studies add environmental sensor
readings, such as air temperature, humidity, and soil chemistry recorded by
Internet of Things devices, to the image in one multimodal model and report that
the fusion model detects diseases and pests more accurately than an image-only
model [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Datasets released for
research supply paired images and sensor readings for training fusion models. A dataset of
subtropical and tropical crop pests and diseases on AI Hub, the Korean
government’s data portal, attaches a panel of soil and ambient sensor variables to
each image and lists predicting disease from that panel among its intended uses [ 6 ] . The Crop Disease Diagnosis (CDD) challenge dataset
pairs each labeled image with an environment series, a time series of greenhouse
sensor readings [ 7 ] . A study on CDD reports that adding
the environment series to a ResNet-50 image classifier raises macro-F1 by
2.58 percentage points [ 8 ] . Whether such
gains come from the plant’s environment depends on what the paired sensor
readings measure.

blocks.en:
A sensor at a farm records a reading at intervals, so a dataset can attach one
reading to every image taken at that farm before the next reading
(Figure 1 A). A reading attached in this way identifies the
farm and the day of acquisition. We call one farm or greenhouse on one day a
session. If disease classes differ between the sessions of a
dataset, a model can predict the class by identifying the session from the
readings, without any agronomic signal in them. The readings are then a shortcut,
which is a feature that predicts the label in the training data but not under new
conditions [ 9 , 10 ] . A random split, however,
tests a model under the conditions of its training data: it places images of one
session in both the training and the test data, so a model can learn in training which class goes
with the readings of each session and recognize the same readings in the test data. A fusion gain measured on a random split therefore cannot separate
an agronomic contribution of the readings from session identity, which makes the session
a confound of the gain.

blocks.en:
Session-disjoint splits, which keep all images of a session on one side and so
would separate the agronomic contribution from session identity, already exist for image
datasets. Image datasets need such splits because the images of one session share
the conditions under which they were taken, so images identify their session
as well. A classifier’s accuracy on the sessions of its training data therefore
need not hold on other sessions: classifiers trained on images taken under controlled
conditions lose accuracy on images taken under other conditions [ 2 , 11 ] . The Global Wheat Head Detection benchmark,
for example, supplies session-disjoint splits that measure that loss. It divides its images into sub-datasets, each of which holds
the images of one experimental unit from one acquisition session [ 12 ] . A
sub-dataset therefore corresponds to one of our sessions, with its experimental
unit as the farm or greenhouse and its acquisition session as the day. The benchmark assigns
each sub-dataset to only one of its training, validation, and test sets [ 12 ] . Its splits therefore measure
accuracy on sessions that the training data do not include. More generally, for data with spatial, temporal, or
hierarchical structure, Roberts et al. [13] recommend
cross-validation that holds out whole blocks of related observations. Session
identity is less apparent in sensor readings than in images, however, because a
sensor reading is a physical measurement and so appears to carry agronomic
information.

The fusion studies that we cite [ 3 , 4 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 8 , 17 , 5 ] apply neither of two checks that would show whether their sensor readings
identify the session. A timestamp, which
is the date and time that a dataset records for each image or for its sensor
reading, identifies the day directly, yet none of the studies compares how well its
sensor readings and a timestamp predict the label. None of the studies reports an
evaluation on a farm-disjoint or session-disjoint split, which keeps all images of
a farm or of a session in either the training or the test data. One of the studies,
however, keeps all image and sensor sequences of each plant or each infection
event (one occurrence of disease) in only one of its training,
validation, and test sets [ 5 ] . That study
states a temporal separation between its training and test data, but its text
does not establish that no session falls on both sides.

blocks.en:
We supply a diagnostic that tests whether a dataset’s sensor readings identify the
session. The diagnostic reads a dataset’s sensor
readings and the metadata that the dataset records for each image, but no image.
Testing a fusion model on held-out farms or sessions, by contrast, needs the
trained model and
needs every class to occur on several farms or sessions, so that each class
appears in both the training and the test data. The diagnostic needs neither, so
it can run before any fusion model is trained. The
diagnostic has two parts (Figure 1 B). A granularity probe
tests whether the sensor readings describe single images or groups of images: it
measures how many images share each sensor reading, how many sessions each
reading occurs in, and the share of each sensor
variable’s variance that farm identity explains. A timestamp baseline predicts the
label from a timestamp alone and compares that prediction with one made from the sensor readings, because a
reading that predicts the label no better than the timestamp may only identify the
session. The timestamp baseline adapts partial-input baselines,
which score a classifier that sees only part of its input and so measure how well
that part alone predicts the label [ 18 ] . Such baselines
have been applied to natural language inference, in which a model decides whether
the second sentence of a pair follows from the first. On the benchmarks of that
task, classifiers that saw only the second sentence still predicted the label, so
the second sentences carried cues to the label [ 19 , 20 ] . Unlike a partial-input
baseline, which keeps part of the model’s input, the timestamp baseline replaces
the sensor readings with the timestamp, so the baseline measures how well the
timestamp alone predicts the label.

blocks.en:
We apply the diagnostic to the AI Hub and CDD datasets and re-analyze the CDD
study on its own split, because the CDD study is the only fusion study that we
cite whose dataset and split were both released. The CDD study also supplies the
fusion model that we train on the AI Hub dataset to test whether the model’s gain
exceeds zero when whole photo dates are held out. Holding out photo dates keeps
the session of most test images out of training, because most images of the AI
Hub dataset were photographed on the day on which their panel was measured. The
test runs on the AI Hub dataset because, unlike CDD, it can be
split by photo date with every class in both the training and the test data. This
paper makes five contributions. • In both datasets, one sensor reading is shared by many images: the AI Hub
dataset carries only 13,150 distinct sets of panel values across a
metadata spreadsheet of 274,000 rows, one row per image, and CDD only
780 distinct environment series for its 5,767 images. • On the AI Hub dataset, a classifier given only the timestamp is
comparable to or better than one given the dataset’s soil-chemistry
readings in
7 of the 7 crops compared. • On the CDD study’s own split, where 91.9% of the test images share
their environment series with training images, a classifier given only the
timestamp reaches the macro-F1 that the study reports for its fusion model. • On CDD, a classifier given only the environment series falls in macro-F1
from 0.885 on a random split to 0.653 on a split that keeps
all images of each series in either the training or the test data, so much of its random-split score comes from
recognizing series seen in training. Under either split, we detect no
difference in macro-F1 between that classifier and one given only the timestamp. • Trained for the CDD study’s 300 epochs, the study’s fusion
model raises macro-F1 relative to an image-only model on a random split of the
AI Hub dataset, but at 5 training runs per model, a test that
holds out whole dates gives confidence intervals too wide to settle whether the
gain exceeds zero on those dates.

blocks.en: 2.1 Datasets
blocks.zh: 2.1 数据集

blocks.en:
The Domestically Cultivated Subtropical and Tropical Pest and Disease Data [ 6 ] , the AI Hub dataset throughout this paper, is
distributed through AI Hub. Its metadata spreadsheet holds 274,000 rows,
each naming one image file whose name encodes the image’s crop, plant part, and
class. Each row also gives the farm, the date and time at which the image was
photographed, the time at which the row’s panel was measured, and a soil and
ambient panel (air temperature, air humidity, soil
moisture, soil temperature, soil pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and
electrical conductivity), although a row can lack some of the panel’s values. The rows span 17 pest and disease classes
and a healthy class across 8 crops: apple mango, banana, dragon fruit,
fig, Hallabong mandarin, lemon, olive, and passion fruit. The dataset
also ships object-detection label files, in which each box marks one lesion or
pest with its class, but every analysis predicts one class per image and so takes each
image’s class from its file name. The usage guideline that accompanies the dataset [ 6 ] records that the environmental sensors were installed per farm and that their readings were
matched to the images afterwards. The images were taken at 24 farms in
August–November 2023. Because a row’s panel can be measured on another day than its
image was photographed, we take the day of a row’s session to be the day on which
its panel was measured, so that all rows that carry one measurement of the panel
fall in one session.

blocks.en: 2.2.1 Granularity probe
blocks.zh: 2.2.1 颗粒探测器

blocks.en:
The granularity probe establishes whether a dataset carries a reading per image or
shares each reading among the images of a farm or a session, whether a shared
reading identifies its session, and whether each sensor variable varies mostly
between farms. To test whether each AI Hub panel variable varies mostly between
farms, we computed the share of its variance that farm identity explains, which is η 2 \eta^{2} of a one-way analysis of
variance with farm as the factor: the between-farm sum of squares divided by the
total sum of squares. Because sessions nest within farms, the share that
sessions explain is at least the share that farm explains, so a variable that
varies mostly between farms varies mostly between sessions as well. We call each
distinct set of a row’s nine panel cells, an empty cell included, a panel tuple. We also counted the
panel tuples, the percentage of rows that share their panel tuple with at least
one other row, and the panel tuples that occur in only one session. To make the
corresponding counts on CDD, we had to decide when two images carry the same
environment series: CDD stamps each row of a series with its reading time, so the
files of two images can differ in their stamps alone. We therefore treated two images as carrying the same
environment series when their CSV files hold identical values once the column of
reading times is dropped. CDD names no greenhouse, so on CDD we approximate a session by the images that
share one series.
We counted the distinct series and the percentage of images that share their
series with another image. To test whether a series identifies one day and one
disease, we also computed two percentages over the series that more than one image
carries: the percentage whose images were all photographed on one date, and the
percentage whose images all carry one disease label, where an image’s disease
label is the disease that its annotation records apart from the crop and the
severity. We read the counts by one rule: a dataset with one distinct reading per image
carries a per-image measurement, whereas a dataset with fewer distinct readings
than images shares its readings. For a dataset that shares its
readings, we take a variable to vary mostly between farms if farm identity
explains more than half of that variable’s variance.

blocks.en: 2.2.2 Timestamp baseline
blocks.zh: 2.2.2 时间戳基线

blocks.en:
The timestamp baseline uses random forests [ 21 ] from
scikit-learn [ 22 ] . One forest predicts each image’s class
from the sensor readings, and another predicts it from the
timestamp alone (the timestamp classifier). On the AI Hub dataset, the timestamp is
the day and the time of day at which a row’s panel was measured, so the timestamp
classifier reads the time of the same reading that the other forest reads.
The day enters as a count of calendar days, whose starting point does not change what a random forest
predicts, and the time of day enters in hours. On the AI Hub dataset, the forest that
reads the sensor readings, which we call the panel classifier, reads only the five
soil-chemistry variables of the panel: pH, N, P, K, and electrical conductivity.
It leaves out the other four panel variables because, within a farm, they change
with the time of day and the season, which the timestamp itself carries, so the comparison sets soil
chemistry against time. We trained and scored both classifiers within each crop,
because 12 of the 17 pest and disease classes
occur on only one crop, so a classifier trained across crops could predict the
class by recognizing the crop. In a crop where one of the five takes a single value, the
classifier also leaves that variable out, because the variable carries no
information in that crop. A crop enters the comparison
of the two classifiers if at least 1,000 of its rows carry all five
variables and those rows span at least two classes. Only the Hallabong mandarin fails this requirement,
because the dataset ships no potassium reading for it. The comparison therefore covers 7 of the dataset’s
8 crops. To bound the computation, we drew 20,000 of the rows that carry all
five variables at random within each crop. Every compared crop has more such rows
than that, so every crop supplies the full draw, and the threshold of
1,000 rows selects the same crops as any threshold up to the draw
size would. We scored every
classifier on the drawn rows by stratified 3-fold cross-validation, which can
place rows of one session in both the training and the test folds, as the random
splits on which fusion gains are reported do. A random seed fixes the random draws of a run, which for the timestamp
baseline are the rows drawn, the folds, and the forest’s random choices. We
repeated the draw and the cross-validation for each of 7 random seeds,
so that every score in the comparison of the two classifiers carries a 95%
confidence interval over seeds. Every classifier used the same
rows, folds, and random seed for its forest, so that the classifiers differ only
in their input columns. A majority-class
predictor, which always predicts the most frequent class of the training folds,
is scored on the same folds and gives the accuracy that a classifier reaches
without any input.

blocks.en:
We scored accuracy and, as a check that no comparison depends on the sizes of
the classes, balanced accuracy. Balanced accuracy is the mean over classes of the
share of each class’s rows that the classifier assigns to that class, so it gives
each class the same weight whatever its size. The timestamp classifier’s margin in a
crop is its accuracy minus the panel classifier’s. We call margins from − 0.02 -0.02{} to + 0.02 +0.02{} the comparable band. The timestamp
classifier is comparable to or better than the panel classifier in a crop if its
margin, averaged over seeds, is at least − 0.02 -0.02{} . Our timestamp criterion
is that the timestamp classifier is comparable to or better than the panel classifier
in a majority of crops. Meeting it would show that in most crops the soil-chemistry
readings predict the class no better than the timestamp, or better by at most the
half-width of the band, so that their accuracy gives no evidence that they do more
than identify the session. We also checked the criterion with no band, counting a
crop only if its mean margin is at least zero, so that the verdict of the criterion does not depend on the width of the band. The criterion uses seed means, so we also report the crops in which the
whole 95% confidence interval of the margin lies outside the band: the timestamp
classifier is superior in such a crop if the interval lies above the band, and the
panel classifier is superior if the interval lies below the band.

3 rows each, after leaving out the rows of the classes below

blocks.en: 2.3 Re-analysis of a published fusion study on CDD
blocks.zh: 2.3 对已发表的关于CDD的聚变研究的再分析

blocks.en:
The CDD study [ 8 ] scores its classifiers by macro-F1,
which is the unweighted mean of the F1 score over classes. The study reports that
adding the environment series to a ResNet-50 image classifier raises macro-F1 from 0.8779 for the image model to 0.9037
for the fusion model [ 8 , Table 2] , the gain of
2.58 percentage points that its abstract quotes. The study obtained both macro-F1 values without its multimodal mixup
augmentation, which adds training examples that blend pairs of examples linearly
in both inputs. Our fusion experiment also leaves that augmentation out. The study’s code is
public [ 23 ] . Of the fusion studies we cite, this study is the
only one whose dataset and evaluation split were both released, so the experiment
behind its fusion claim can be re-run outside its author list.

blocks.en:
We measured how much of the study’s test set shares its environment series with
training. The study states a ratio of training, validation, and test images but
not how it drew its split, so we took the split from the study’s repository,
which ships the split files themselves. The repository ships two sets of image
identifiers that each list the identifiers of a training, a validation, and a test
partition. The study’s training script reads
one of the two sets, so the measurements below refer to that set, the study’s
split, unless they name the other set, whose partitions hold the ratio that the
study states. We matched its identifiers
to the environment series and computed the leak rate, the share of test images
whose series also occurs in training. Dropping the column of reading times can only merge files into one series,

blocks.en:
To test whether a classifier predicts CDD’s classes by recognizing environment
series that it saw in training, we drew two splits ourselves, each over 7 random seeds. Each seed divides the images into 7 folds and holds out one fold for
testing. The folds are stratified by class alone (the random split) or also
grouped by environment series, so that each series, and so each CDD session, falls in exactly one fold (the
group-disjoint split). On the random and group-disjoint
splits, random forests with the settings of the timestamp baseline predict the 25-class label from
the environment series (the environment classifier), from the day and the time of
day of the photograph (the timestamp classifier), and from both. A majority-class
predictor is scored on the same test images. The environment features are the
mean, minimum, maximum, and first and last non-missing values of each value column of
the series. Missing values are imputed by the median of the training images. Our criterion for a classifier that recognizes series seen in training is that the
environment classifier loses more than 0.03 macro-F1 on the
group-disjoint split relative to the random split. Because the threshold is our
choice, we also report whether the environment classifier’s interval on the
group-disjoint split lies entirely below its interval on the random split. A split by series can leave a
test image’s photo date in training, so we also checked whether CDD admits a
split by date. We took each calendar month after the first as a test
block whose training data are the earlier months. In each crop whose images carry
at least two disease labels, counting healthy as one label, a test block kept the
test images whose disease label also occurs in the earlier months. We counted the
test blocks that keep images of at least two disease labels, because only such a
block can test whether a classifier separates diseases.

blocks.en:
The fusion experiment asks whether the fusion model of the CDD study produces a
gain on the AI Hub dataset, and whether the gain still exceeds zero on a split that holds out
time. Only a dataset in which a date-disjoint split leaves every class on both
sides can test whether the gain exceeds zero on such a split. A date-disjoint split of the AI Hub
dataset keeps every class on both sides, whereas no date-disjoint split of CDD can,
because 4 of its 25 classes were photographed on a single
date (Section 3.4 ).

We compared 4 candidate splits to choose the unit
that the experiment holds out. The candidates were a random split and splits
disjoint by farm, by photo date, and by the pair of farm and photo date. For
9.3% of the rows, the image was photographed on another day than
the one on which the row’s panel was measured, so a split by photo date can place
rows that share one session’s panel in both the training and the test data. For each split, we divided the whole metadata spreadsheet into 5
folds, at random or by the split’s unit, and measured two quantities averaged over
the folds. The leak rate, defined as on CDD, is the share of test images whose panel tuple
recurs in training, so a high leak rate lets a model recognize a test image’s
session from its panel. Coverage is the share of test images whose combination of crop, plant
part (the organ photographed), and class also occurs in training. A split low in
coverage measures how the models handle unseen combinations rather than what the
panel contributes, so we set a floor of 80% on
coverage. A
random split has a leak rate of 99.3%, so it leaves the panel tuple of
nearly every test image in training. A farm-disjoint split has a
leak rate of zero but covers only 72.6% of its test images, below that floor.
The splits disjoint by photo date and by the pair of farm and photo date have
leak rates of 7.2% and 7.7% and cover every test image, so any floor
above the farm-disjoint split’s coverage keeps these two splits and excludes the
farm-disjoint one. The experiment
holds out photo dates. The splits by photo date and by the pair of farm and photo
date both keep together the images of each farm and photo date, but only the split
by photo date also keeps each test image’s photo date out of training.

blocks.en:
The fusion experiment trains an image-only model and a fusion model on a
subsample of the AI Hub dataset, which we drew to bound the training cost:
40,000 images stratified by crop, plant part, and class. Besides the
date-disjoint split, we kept a farm-disjoint split although its coverage falls
below the floor, because the date-disjoint split still shares farms between its
training and test images. We split the subsample three ways, each holding out one
of 5 folds for testing: at random (the in-distribution split), by
photo date (date-disjoint), and by farm (farm-disjoint). The test images of the
in-distribution split share farms and dates with its training images. We report
the farm-disjoint gain beside its coverage. A
validation set was drawn from the training images by the same grouping as the
test images, to choose the epoch whose weights were kept. An epoch is one pass
over the training images. The image-only model is a
ResNet-50 [ 24 ] pretrained on ImageNet [ 25 ] ,
taken from the timm library [ 26 ] . The fusion model is a late
fusion, which combines the class scores (logits) of the ResNet-50 with those of
an environmental branch in a fusion layer. The branch and the fusion layer are
the CDD study’s own, taken from the model file that its repository releases [ 23 ] . We resized the output layers of the branch and of the
fusion layer to this dataset’s classes. The branch is a long short-term memory (LSTM) network [ 27 ] , a recurrent network for sequences, followed by two
fully connected layers. The fusion layer randomly zeroes a share of the two sets
of class scores during training (dropout), joins them into one vector, and maps
that vector to the classes with a fully connected layer. The branch was written
for a time series, whereas each AI Hub image carries a single set of panel values, so the branch
reads a sequence of length one. Unlike the panel classifier, the branch reads all nine panel variables, because
the experiment tests the panel as a fusion model receives it.
A missing value is set to zero, as in the CDD study’s code. Each variable is
then scaled to the unit interval by its minimum and maximum over the training
images.

blocks.en:
Both models follow the CDD study’s training procedure
in its augmentation of the training images by random transformations, its
sampling of training images in inverse proportion to their class frequency, its
Adam optimizer [ 28 ] , its schedule for the optimizer’s learning
rate, and its selection of the weights from the epoch with the best validation
macro-F1. The learning rate is the step size of the optimizer’s weight updates.
The schedule, cosine annealing with warm restarts, lowers the rate along a
cosine curve and returns it to its initial value at fixed intervals [ 29 ] . To bound the computation, we first trained both models
on all three splits at a reduced budget that departs from the study’s procedure in
three settings: 40 epochs, batches of 64 images,
and early stopping, which ends a run once the validation score stops improving.
We then trained both models on
the in-distribution and date-disjoint splits at the matched budget, the study’s
own 300 epochs with batches of 8 images and no early
stopping, because the interval of the in-distribution gain included zero at the
reduced budget and a reduced budget can undertrain the environmental branch. We
did not retrain on the farm-disjoint split at the matched budget, because its
coverage falls below the floor and its gain therefore measures in part how the models handle unseen
combinations of crop, plant part, and class at any budget.

counts of distinct readings, the fusion results at the matched budget, and every
comparison that uses those counts or the comparable band. These comparisons are
the timestamp comparison on the AI Hub dataset, the within-session measurement, and
the comparison of the random and group-disjoint splits on CDD, whose
group-disjoint split groups the images by distinct environment series. By
contrast, the criterion on the CDD study’s split and the criteria of the fusion
experiment do not depend on the five parts, although the fusion experiment’s
results at the matched budget do. The leak rates of the two sets of identifiers
that the CDD study’s repository ships and of the AI Hub splits do not depend on
the five parts either, because a leak rate is a share of test images, whereas the
counts of distinct readings and the group-disjoint split take each distinct
reading as a unit. Nor does any rule of ours for matching sensor values change
these leak rates: on CDD, matching the raw files gives the same rates on both sets
of identifiers, because nearly
every series that images share is stored in identical files, stamps included;
on the AI Hub dataset, a leak rate needs no matching rule, because a panel tuple
holds a row’s nine cells as the spreadsheet records them, an empty cell included.

blocks.en: 4 Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论

blocks.en: 4.1 The sensor readings of both datasets identify the session
blocks.zh: 4.1 国家 两个数据集的传感器读取可确定会话

blocks.en:
The readings that the two datasets attach to their images mainly identify the session
rather than measure each plant’s environment. Most of the predictive
value of the AI Hub dataset’s soil-chemistry readings is farm and session
identity, because restricting prediction to one session removes most of the
panel classifier’s advantage on average across crops. A timestamp is also
comparable to or better than those readings at predicting the class, so their
accuracy over a whole crop gives no evidence that they do more than identify the
session. Within a session, by contrast, the residual advantage exceeds the
half-width of the comparable band in every crop, so the soil-chemistry readings still
separate classes within a session. The readings can separate classes within a
session without measuring the plant’s environment, however, because a reading
within a session can be attached to the images taken until the next reading and
so identify the part of the day in which they were taken.

blocks.en: 4.3 Recommendations for fusion studies and dataset releases
blocks.zh: 4.3 关于聚变研究和数据集释放的建议

blocks.en:
A fusion study on a paired image–sensor dataset should report two things. The
first is its fusion gain on a farm- or session-disjoint split. Every fusion study
needs this split, because the confound that it controls for arose through a
different mechanism in each of two datasets assembled by separate groups: on the
AI Hub dataset, readings from sensors installed per farm and matched to the images
afterwards, and on CDD, per-image files that repeat one environment series across
many images. A study
therefore cannot rule the confound out by checking for one mechanism. The second is the score of a
sensor-only model, set beside the scores of a majority-class predictor and a
timestamp classifier on the same test set and metric. The timestamp classifier is needed
beside the majority-class predictor because a sensor-only accuracy far above the
majority-class accuracy is not by itself evidence of agronomic signal: session
identity alone can produce it on a split that shares sessions. Some of the fusion studies we cite publish a sensor-only score, but none sets
a majority-class score beside it, so a reader cannot tell how far those
scores exceed the majority-class score. Berrocal et al. [17] give their soil-moisture-only baseline its own subsection
and table, yet even they interpret that baseline’s accuracy as “a meaningful but
limited level of discrimination” relative to their image model rather than to a
majority-class predictor.

blocks.en: 4.4 Limitations and future work
blocks.zh: 4.4 限制和今后的工作

blocks.en:
Neither dataset that we examined has sensor readings known to carry agronomic
signal, so we have shown that the diagnostic finds confounded datasets but not
that it separates them from unconfounded ones. Showing that would need a dataset
that records a variable known to drive the disease at the plant and time of each
image. The diagnostic also cannot certify a
dataset on which it finds no confound, because a partial input that fails to
predict the label does not show that no label cue exists [ 18 ] . The timestamp baseline uses random forests and the
fusion experiment one fusion architecture, the CDD study’s late fusion, so neither
sets an upper bound on what a stronger learner could extract from the sensor
readings. A date-disjoint test that settles whether the AI Hub fusion gain in
macro-F1 exceeds zero on held-out dates needs more random seeds than we ran. On CDD,
we ran no split that holds out whole photo dates, which would remove the photo-date
confound for every class but the 4 photographed on a single
date. Both
datasets come from Korean farms and greenhouses, so the extent of the confound in
datasets collected elsewhere remains to be measured.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
Studies that fuse crop images with environmental sensor readings report gains on
paired datasets without establishing what the readings measure. We tested whether
the readings identify the session with a diagnostic that reads no image. In both Korean datasets
that we examined, nearly every image shares its sensor reading with other images.
A timestamp alone is comparable to or better than the soil-chemistry readings in
every crop of the AI Hub dataset that we compared. On CDD, neither the timestamp
nor the environment series predicts the class better than the other in macro-F1
under either split that we draw. In
the split of a published CDD fusion study, 91.9% of the test images share
their environment series with training images. On that split, a timestamp alone matches the macro-F1 that the
study reports for its fusion model. A late-fusion gain on the AI Hub
dataset replicates in distribution when the models are trained for the CDD
study’s 300 epochs, but whether it exceeds zero in macro-F1 on held-out
dates remains unresolved at the seed count we ran. On both datasets, the diagnostic
finds that the readings mainly identify the session, so a fusion study can show what
its readings add to the image only on a farm- or session-disjoint split.
